title: Nearly linear-time solution of general sparse linear systems
formal:
For every fixed integer \(c\ge1\), do there exist a uniform randomized classical algorithm \(A_c\) and constants \(C_c,K_c\ge1\), \(d_c\ge0\), all integers, with the following guarantee? Every promised input consists of \(n\ge2\), a nonsingular rational matrix \(A\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n}\) with \(m\) nonzero entries, a nonzero vector \(b\in\mathbb Q^n\), and an integer \(1\le p\le c\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\). Every input numerator magnitude and positive denominator has at most \(c\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\) binary digits, and
\[\kappa_2(A)\le n^c.\]
On every run, \(A_c\) must halt within
\[C_c m\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil^{d_c}\]
word operations in the model below, with word length \(w=K_c\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\). With probability at least \(2/3\), its explicit rational output \(\widehat x\in\mathbb Q^n\) must satisfy
\[\|A\widehat x-b\|_2\le2^{-p}\|b\|_2.\]
The constants and the finite program may depend on \(c\), but must work for all promised dimensions, matrices, right-hand sides and accuracies. Matrices may be nonsymmetric and indefinite.
definitions:
The input explicitly gives \(n,m,p\) in binary, followed by an unordered list of \(m\) triples consisting of a row index, a column index and a nonzero rational value, with distinct positions in \(\{1,\ldots,n\}^2\), and then all \(n\) entries of \(b\). Unlisted matrix entries are zero. Rational numbers are signed binary integer numerators and positive binary integer denominators; reduced fractions are not required. The binary length of zero is one, and a sign is stored separately. Fixed separators specify the list boundaries and integer lengths. Nonsingularity implies \(n\le m\le n^2\), so the total encoding has \(O_c(m\log n)\) bits. The parameter \(c\) specifies the family of promises, rather than an additional runtime input. The algorithm need not verify the promises; guarantees are required only on inputs satisfying them.

For a real vector \(z\), \(\|z\|_2=(\sum_i z_i^2)^{1/2}\). Define \(\sigma_{\max}(A)=\max_{\|z\|_2=1}\|Az\|_2\), \(\sigma_{\min}(A)=\min_{\|z\|_2=1}\|Az\|_2\), and \(\kappa_2(A)=\sigma_{\max}(A)/\sigma_{\min}(A)\). The minimum is positive for nonsingular \(A\). The requested error is relative residual error for this exact rational input, with \(\varepsilon=2^{-p}\). It is not a promise that the approximate vector has the same relative forward error as the residual.

The word RAM has a fixed finite program and a fixed finite number of registers, each holding an unsigned \(w\)-bit word. Input is stored as an explicit binary string packed into a read-only word array. Working memory consists of \(w\)-bit cells addressed by \(w\)-bit words and initially zero; no input-dependent advice or precomputed table is supplied. A step performs one read or write, comparison, conditional branch, addition, subtraction or multiplication modulo \(2^w\), unsigned quotient or remainder with a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operation, or logical shift of a word. A shift by at least \(w\) positions returns zero. Address computations use the same instructions. One fresh independent uniform \(w\)-bit word costs one step. Longer integers occupy multiple cells and use multiple operations. No instruction acts on an arbitrary real number or arbitrary-length integer at unit cost.

The output is a length-delimited explicit list of \(n\) signed binary numerators and positive binary denominators. Every output word must be written, and all its bits occupy the output encoding. Input processing, preprocessing, any auxiliary matrices, numerical precision, randomness and output cost are included in the stated time bound. The clock is a worst-case bound on every choice of random words, not an expected bound. Probability refers only to the algorithm's independent randomness for each fixed input. An invalid output counts as failure. Uniformity means one program for each fixed \(c\), without dependence on \(n\) or on the particular input; no extra effective procedure generating programs from \(c\) is requested.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition, or of its full logical negation, in this word-RAM model. An affirmative proof must establish the algorithm, its worst-case clock and its success guarantee for every fixed \(c\) and every input in the associated promise family. A negative proof must establish that for some fixed \(c\), no finite program and constants satisfy all these guarantees. It must exclude all algorithms in the stated model, rather than only a chosen iterative method or preconditioner. A result restricted to one structured matrix family, a different output representation or an uncharged real-arithmetic model does not meet the target.
why: This tests whether sparsity and moderate conditioning suffice for solving linear equations at essentially the cost of reading them. A resolution would clarify the limits of graph-based solvers, preconditioning and numerical subroutines used throughout algorithms and optimization.

importance.reason: A fundamental input-size complexity question for one of the most widely used computational primitives, with meaningful positive results for structured classes and general reductions from apparently special systems.

progress.text: Spielman and Teng establish nearly linear expected-time solvers for symmetric diagonally dominant systems, with an energy-norm guarantee and a finite-precision analysis; the expanded solver paper appears in 2014.

Peng and Vempala give a general finite-precision sparse solver faster than matrix multiplication in suitable sparsity regimes; preprint v2 is dated 7 January 2021 and the conference version is SODA 2021.
Nie improves the matrix anti-concentration result and the associated sparse-system running time; the current preprint is v2 from 2 December 2021 and the conference version is STOC 2022.
The ICALP paper establishes sparse-linear-equation completeness for Laplacians of two-dimensional simplicial complexes.
The Peng–Vempala work appears in JACM; this publication does not replace the near-linear target by the already achieved matrix-multiplication improvement.
Version 3 of the Simons workshop report records status through 20 August and retains broader scalable-solver and finite-precision questions.

status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The retained proposition is an explicitly editorial near-linear target, not a named conjecture or the already resolved faster-than-matrix-multiplication question. Inspected primary results improve general polynomial bounds or handle structured families; the August 2026 report retains narrower scalable-solver and finite-precision questions. Bounded later-work searches found no matching universal solver or unconditional impossibility proof. This status assessment does not independently certify the cited proofs.

context_blocks.text: Sparse linear equations are a basic subroutine in optimization and scientific computation. A matrix with \(m\) nonzeros can be stored without its \(n^2-m\) zero entries, and multiplying it by a vector requires only a small amount of arithmetic per stored coefficient. Whether solving the system can have comparable worst-case cost is a stronger question. Moderate conditioning controls numerical sensitivity, but does not itself supply an efficient solver.

Residual error and solution error are different. With \(x^*=A^{-1}b\),
\[\frac{\|\widehat x-x^*\|_2}{\|x^*\|_2}\le\kappa_2(A)\frac{\|A\widehat x-b\|_2}{\|b\|_2}.\]
For example, \(A=\operatorname{diag}(1,\delta)\), \(b=(1,\delta)\) and \(\widehat x=(1,0)\), for \(0<\delta<1\), have absolute residual \(\delta\) even though the second solution coordinate is wrong by one. The card fixes the norm, conditioning and requested tolerance so that these distinct accuracy notions are not conflated.

Spielman and Teng obtain nearly linear expected-time algorithms for symmetric diagonally dominant matrices, whose diagonal entries satisfy \(A_{ii}\ge\sum_{j\ne i}|A_{ij}|\). Their error guarantee uses the energy norm \(\|z\|_A=(z^{\mathsf T}Az)^{1/2}\). Their paper also analyzes finite precision. For positive-definite inputs, comparison with the Euclidean residual depends on conditioning. These results establish the importance of structural assumptions; their stated norm and expected-time convention are not identical to this card's general guarantee.

Peng and Vempala's SODA 2021 theorem gives a general finite-precision solver that beats matrix-multiplication time for sufficiently sparse, polynomially conditioned systems. The theorem measures residual relative to the projection of the right-hand side onto the column space; for the nonsingular square inputs here, that projection is simply \(b\). The work later appears in JACM in 2025. Asking only to beat the matrix-multiplication barrier would therefore miss the remaining near-linear question.

Nie's 2022 result improves the general bound to
\[\widetilde O\!\left(m^{(\omega-2)/(\omega-1)}n^2\right)\]
in the polynomial-conditioning and precision regime. Here \(\omega\) denotes the matrix-multiplication exponent and \(\widetilde O\) suppresses polylogarithmic factors. For \(m=\widetilde O(n)\), the displayed bound becomes \(\widetilde O(n^{(3\omega-4)/(\omega-1)})\). This remains well above near-linear time; the historical numerical exponent printed in the paper is tied to the matrix-multiplication bound then available.

Ding, Kyng, Probst Gutenberg and Zhang show that linear equations in Laplacians of two-dimensional simplicial complexes are sparse-linear-equation complete. Their reduction preserves sparsity up to logarithmic factors and has polynomial effects on coefficient sizes, conditioning and requested accuracy for the stated integer-input family. Thus apparently structured higher-dimensional systems already capture substantial general difficulty. This is a reduction between solver tasks, not an unconditional lower bound ruling out a near-linear algorithm.

The August 2026 Simons workshop report discusses scalable solvers for parameterized partial-differential-equation benchmarks, preconditioning, and finite-precision iterative methods. Those questions distinguish guarantees for a selected family from a universal guarantee over sparse inputs. They also distinguish iteration counts from a full cost accounting. The report supplies contemporary context rather than a theorem settling the editorial target here.

The output is part of the computational task. Writing \(n\) approximate coordinates is compatible with near-linear sparse-input time because \(m\ge n\). Returning selected observables, oracle access to an implicit vector, or a quantum state changes that requirement. Requiring the exact rational solution instead would also change the question by introducing potentially much larger coordinate encodings. The stated word model charges storage and processing of all precision actually used.

sentences: A sparse linear system explicitly stores only the nonzero matrix entries and its right-hand side.
The question asks whether every nonsingular rational system with polynomial conditioning can be approximately solved in nearly linear time in the number of nonzeros.
Coefficient lengths and residual accuracy are bounded on a logarithmic scale, and the output must list every rational coordinate.
The fixed word-RAM model charges preprocessing, precision, randomness and output, with a worst-case time bound and success probability at least two thirds.
Known structured solvers and general improvements over matrix multiplication motivate the target but do not provide its universal near-linear guarantee.

source_formulation.text: This is the retained editorial near-input-size variant of the general sparse-system complexity question. Polynomial conditioning, logarithmic input coefficient lengths, inverse-polynomial residual accuracy, an explicit rational output and the word-RAM cost convention make the broad direction precise. Peng–Vempala and Nie supply the general finite-precision context; the Simons workshop report asks narrower benchmark and numerical-analysis questions. The proposition is not attributed to a numbered conjecture in that report, and does not ask the already resolved question of beating matrix multiplication.
